en: Abiding by the sūtras spoken by Ātreya, I shall set forth the unchanging words in the form of verses for the ease of those who study well:
"Niṣkaivalya, Niṣṭarkya, from the Niṣādas, Niṣaṅgadhī."
And the most exhilarating [Soma] called upon Mahiman and Niṣkagra for slaughter;
the Aśvatara with the Vatsataras, the Kikidivi, and Vidīgaya [seized] Upahatnu and the ninety-fold Phaliga made of gold.
With his soft-bellied [bow], beautifying the *iḍabṛd* [hymns] while bellowing loudly,
he took from Gautama the sovereignty over the Saudāsas;
and the infinite, hornless one again [took] the high and low Apsarases.
Like Aṅgiras, may the chameleon, the krumuka wood,
and the fire-god consume the smoke-colored taint; and may the biting serpents,
together with the gods, sweeten the jaundice at this first purification from sin.
On the day following the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, with this [hymn],
one should offer a cock that resembles a *kṛka*, whose beak resembles a *datīkāśa*, which is not coarse,
and which expands with its own body; and on the preceding day, one should offer a lotus-garland.
And [he offered] the *duṣṭarītu* with the *kakubha* verses, as well as the *codaka*;
the *nābhānediṣṭha* from the *āgnīdhra*, and the *sarṇīkā* and *sanīti*;
and having churned with the cows for the two *gopas*, he offered to *Gopāya* and to *Giriśa*.
And he who possesses horns not born of a cow, who is ever-yielding and unsolicited,
will make people blind with tears and devoid of luster;
while Vasuka, the thundering cloud that endures, shall be without blessings.
The Nīcakāra approached, seeking booty; and Uccāditis came as well.
Paracchepas, Cakravāka, and Kṛṣamāṇa were adorned; Acchāvāka was there, and the Kapardins were listening and shining. 11–12.
To Mānthīlava, to Dacāvarta, to Gabheya, to Canohita, and to Pākalāya— his horns are extended for Prāsaca;
to Vaiśanta, to Avārya, to Nīhāra, and likewise to Āyu.
The wise ones carry [the oblation] from eleven layers;
the two spouses bestow eighty-fold strength and wide dominion upon the kidneys; having circumambulated, Trasadasyu and Duṣṭara shall be proclaimed. 14–15.

The resident [priest] [recites] "Śunaḥśepam," "sāsahyāma," "priyaṅgavaḥ," "antarikṣāt," "cāpayitā," "naktayā," and "kapardine" (verse 16). In the subsequent section (anuvāka), those words beginning with the letter *da* are found in that [same] position.
For the sake of the seed-bearing [organ], that is desired as the non-masculine.
The powerful one yokes the son of Ajīgarta and the bird; for it has risen from the two kidneys and the two tendons, O you who possess the downward slope. 17–18.

The low-voiced sound increasing everywhere, the impotent one, the seeker of wealth, the Atharvans, and the son of the two cows for the sake of friendlessness— [these are] for the wise one with Gāyatrī verses and for the giver with Jagatī verses.
Seeking him out and bestowing him, and guarding the vigorous steed,
the Lord of Mightiness, as he is being born, looks upon him according to his due measure for the sake of victory and for the one about to be born, as they fly toward him.
The Svarṇara, Jīvanasvāyī, Vṛṣadakṣa, Salāvṛkī, and Surabhi— along with these, the Viniśruti is for our well-being.
And from there, the Dṛśīkas purify themselves before the Maruts.
And Vivasvān is common [to all], and we have harmed [them] for the sake of prosperity (23). Having consecrated [them]— thus everywhere, while bearing [the burden]—
[he recites] the four beginning with *ayākya* as before, and likewise the verse beginning with *svadhitiḥ* (24).
For one such as this, there are four [types of] sacrificial sessions for the wise:
the Ārghya, the Uṣitvā, the Prāvṛtā, and likewise the Bījakā and Pippakā.
From the Ambarīṣa comes Amīvā, and from the Ambarīṣa comes the Dundubhi.
With the [hymn] belonging to the three realms, may they be immortal and most tireless for all;
with the breath of all, crushing the iron [fortress],
may the Vaikaṅkatī, the Sārdigṛdī, and the Āśubhā [songs] shatter it.
The Ātreya Śikṣā is complete;
now begins the third part of the Ātreya Śikṣā.

Now, regarding the first two verses: since the *jaṭā* [interwoven arrangement] arises from the sequential, non-sequential, and transposed orders of vowels produced by Vedic (*ārṣaja*) and euphonic (*saṃdhija*) sandhi, I shall elucidate it for the delight of the learned after having respectfully examined the *Śikṣā* and other relevant works. (1)

"The sign of the two words would be [the absence] of one; however, in that case, it should be understood as being like *saṃhitā* in its sequence. In the same way, the *jaṭā* should be understood by the wise. This is the final verse.
"A wise person should first establish the secondness of the first;
in the case of *dhūdvakṣṇau* and *dvandvakṣṇaṣam*, the *anusvāra* is [treated] according to its own nature," so says the Ātreya-Śikṣā.
